paragraphs.text: New Rainbow is a [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from Yunnan, kept as loose leaf rather than pressed. It begins as leaf from the province’s large-leaf trees, picked and withered, then fried in a wok to [kill the green](sheng:making) and dried in the sun. The leaf is never hot-air dried, and that is the point: some of its own activity survives the wok, which is what lets the tea go on changing. What comes out is [maocha](sheng:processing), the rough tea that is either sold loose, as this one is, or pressed.

Sheng is given none of the rapid fermentation that makes shou, so it changes slowly, over years, as it is [stored](sheng:aging). How and where a tea is kept becomes part of its history, though good storage does not promise a good tea.

brewing.text: Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: In young raw pu’er, a bitter, drying bite that turns into a returning sweetness, a feel in the throat that makes the mouth water, and fresh, floral or fruity notes such as apricot or plum. Tea kept in humid storage can carry a damp, earthy storage taste.
